1 What this note settles

CLEANSER (Liu et al. 2025) models per-guide ambient gRNA counts with a Negative Binomial (NB) and shows, in its Figure 3B, that in the direct-capture barnyard experiment the ground-truth ambient is strongly overdispersed (variance \(\gg\) mean), whereas in the CROP-seq experiment it sits on the Poisson line. fishash / geomux instead assume a Poisson / hypergeometric ambient null. These look contradictory.

This note shows, entirely from the raw barnyard counts and with every number produced by executable code, that:

  1. CLEANSER’s Fig 3B reproduces — direct-capture per-guide ambient really is overdispersed (median var/mean \(\approx 10\)); CROP-seq really is Poisson (var/mean \(\approx 1\)).
  2. The overdispersion is doublet-driven. A right tail of cells carry a whole wrong-species cell’s worth of gRNA UMIs (co-encapsulated doublets), and the top 1% of cells account for \(\approx 98.5\%\) of the excess variance.
  3. Removing gRNA-channel doublets collapses Fig 3B onto the Poisson line — the per-guide variance-vs-mean cloud pulls back onto \(\mathrm{var}=\mathrm{mean}\), and a direct, bootstrap-calibrated goodness-of-fit test (§Part 4) cannot distinguish the de-doubleted direct-capture ambient from \(\mathrm{Poisson}(a_g\,d_c)\): observed Pearson \(\phi = 0.993\) sits squarely inside the Poisson null band \([0.956, 1.018]\) (\(p\approx 0.25\)). The rank-1 mean \(\lambda_{gc}=R_g C_c/T\) captures the structure; what little pooled var/mean excess remains is 1–5 cut-boundary doublet entries, not smooth soup overdispersion. The authors’ own GEX-purity knob does the same thing, more weakly.

Both papers are correct on their own terms. The only difference is whether doublets are removed from the gRNA channel before dispersion is measured. The de-doubleted ambient — the object fishash’s null actually applies to — is indistinguishable from Poisson to the resolution the data allow (§Part 4 puts a formal test and honest power bounds on that claim).

2 Data and definitions

We use the non-co-cultured 0hr barnyard experiment from Liu et al. 2025 (GSE272457), which is the sample CLEANSER’s Fig 3B is built on. It was assayed with two chemistries, direct-capture and CROP-seq, giving a clean within-dataset contrast. Both are exported (guides \(\times\) cells, MatrixMarket) alongside per-cell gene-expression (GEX) metadata and a guide\(\to\)library map.

Per-cell metadata and the species call. The metadata gives, per cell, the summed GEX UMIs mapping to the human transcriptome (homo_sum_gex) and the mouse transcriptome (mus_sum_gex), plus mitochondrial and feature counts used for QC. A cell’s species is called from GEX, independently of any gRNA. Crucially, these exports have no QC or species filtering applied — QC is downstream and is exactly the knob we will exercise.

2.1 Explicit definitions used throughout

  • Species call (GEX-purity \(p\)). A cell is human if homo_sum_gex > mus_sum_gex and the majority-species fraction of GEX \(\ge p\); mouse analogously. The authors’ QC uses \(p = 0.90\). This \(p\) is the authors’ own doublet/ambient-purity knob (a cell that is 50/50 human/mouse GEX is a GEX doublet and is excluded).
  • Ground-truth ambient. The count of a wrong-species guide in a host-species cell — e.g. a mouse-library guide in a human cell. That guide was never integrated into that cell, so any UMIs are ambient contamination (or a co-encapsulated cell). This is the object both papers model.
  • CLEANSER Fig 3B statistic. For each wrong-species guide, the mean and variance of its UMI counts across all host-species cells, including the zeros. Because most host cells have zero ambient UMIs of a given guide, per-guide means are tiny (\(\sim 0.005\)–\(0.3\)). Plot variance vs mean; the line var = mean is the Poisson expectation.
  • gRNA-channel doublet score. For a cell, \(\text{wrong\_frac} = \dfrac{\text{wrong-species gRNA UMIs}}{\text{total gRNA UMIs}}\). A cell whose gRNA pool is mostly wrong-species is not “ambient” — it is a co-encapsulated wrong-species cell (a doublet). This is a gRNA-channel purity measure, independent of the GEX-purity QC.

2.2 Loading + QC (verbatim from the authors’ pipeline)

The QC below is transcribed from the authors’ barnyard_io.R, with GEX-purity \(p\) exposed as the only free knob. Everything downstream calls load_sample().

Code 
# Authors' GEX QC (verbatim), purity p as the only knob.
barnyard_qc <- function(meta, purity = 0.9) {
  sum_gex   <- meta$homo_sum_gex + meta$mus_sum_gex
  frac_homo <- meta$homo_sum_gex / sum_gex
  qc <- (meta$mito_sum / sum_gex < .15) & (meta$features_gex <= 6000) &
        (sum_gex <= 20000) & (meta$features_gex >= 1500) & (sum_gex >= 3500) &
        (frac_homo < (1 - purity) | frac_homo > purity)
  qc[is.na(qc)] <- FALSE
  list(qc = qc, frac_homo = frac_homo)
}

load_sample <- function(sample, purity = 0.9) {
  gm     <- as(readMM(file.path(REPRO, paste0(sample, "_grna_counts.mtx"))), "CsparseMatrix")
  meta   <- read.csv(file.path(REPRO, paste0(sample, "_meta.csv")))
  guides <- read.csv(file.path(REPRO, paste0(sample, "_guides.csv")))
  stopifnot(nrow(meta) == ncol(gm), nrow(guides) == nrow(gm))
  q <- barnyard_qc(meta, purity = purity)
  counts <- gm[, q$qc, drop = FALSE]
  rownames(counts) <- guides$guide
  guide_homo <- guides$guide_type == "homo_guide"   # TRUE = human-library guide
  cell_homo  <- q$frac_homo[q$qc] > purity           # TRUE = pure human cell
  list(counts = counts, guide_homo = guide_homo, cell_homo = cell_homo,
       frac_homo = q$frac_homo[q$qc], purity = purity,
       chemistry = if (grepl("Cropseq", sample)) "CROP-seq" else "direct-capture",
       sample = sample)
}

# Wrong-species (ambient) mask: guide species != cell species.
amb_mask_of <- function(obj) {
  m <- outer(obj$guide_homo, obj$cell_homo, function(g, c) g != c)
  as(Matrix(m, sparse = TRUE), "lgCMatrix")
}

3 Part 1 — Reproduce CLEANSER Figure 3B

We compute the Fig-3B statistic exactly: per wrong-species guide, the mean and (sample) variance of its UMI counts across all host-species cells, including zeros.

Code 
# Per-guide (mean, var, var/mean) of a wrong-species guide block across
# host-species cells, INCLUDING zeros. focus picks the direction.
cleanser_perguide <- function(obj, focus = c("mus_in_homo", "homo_in_mus"),
                              cell_subset = NULL) {
  focus   <- match.arg(focus)
  cnt     <- obj$counts
  cellsel <- if (is.null(cell_subset)) rep(TRUE, ncol(cnt)) else cell_subset
  if (focus == "mus_in_homo") {          # mouse-library guides across human cells
    gsel <- !obj$guide_homo
    csel <- obj$cell_homo & cellsel
  } else {                                # human-library guides across mouse cells
    gsel <- obj$guide_homo
    csel <- (!obj$cell_homo) & cellsel
  }
  sub <- cnt[gsel, csel, drop = FALSE]    # ambient guides x host-species cells
  nC  <- ncol(sub)
  s1  <- Matrix::rowSums(sub)             # per-guide sum over ALL nC cells
  s2  <- Matrix::rowSums(sub * sub)
  mu  <- s1 / nC
  v   <- (s2 - nC * mu^2) / (nC - 1)      # sample variance, incl. the zeros
  data.frame(guide = rownames(sub), mean = mu, var = v,
             vmr = ifelse(mu > 0, v / mu, NA_real_), n_cells = nC, focus = focus)
}

# Pooled var/mean over EVERY wrong-species (guide, cell) entry incl. zeros.
pooled_vmr <- function(obj, cell_subset = NULL) {
  mask <- amb_mask_of(obj); cnt <- obj$counts
  if (!is.null(cell_subset)) {
    cnt <- cnt[, cell_subset, drop = FALSE]; mask <- mask[, cell_subset, drop = FALSE]
  }
  vals <- (cnt * mask)[mask]              # every masked entry, incl. zeros
  list(mean = mean(vals), var = var(vals), vmr = var(vals) / mean(vals),
       n = length(vals), n_nz = sum(vals > 0), max = max(vals))
}
Code 
dc <- load_sample("mix0hr_DirectCapture", 0.90)  # authors' QC
cs <- load_sample("mix0hr_Cropseq", 0.90)

summ <- do.call(rbind, list(
  cbind(sample = "DirectCapture", dir = "mouse-in-human",
        (function(pg) data.frame(n_guides = nrow(pg),
          mean_lo = min(pg$mean), mean_hi = max(pg$mean),
          median_vmr = median(pg$vmr, na.rm = TRUE),
          pct_above = 100 * mean(pg$var > pg$mean, na.rm = TRUE),
          pooled_vmr = sum(pg$var) / sum(pg$mean)))(cleanser_perguide(dc, "mus_in_homo"))),
  cbind(sample = "DirectCapture", dir = "human-in-mouse",

          mean_lo = min(pg$mean), mean_hi = max(pg$mean),
          median_vmr = median(pg$vmr, na.rm = TRUE),
          pct_above = 100 * mean(pg$var > pg$mean, na.rm = TRUE),

  cbind(sample = "CROP-seq", dir = "mouse-in-human",
        (function(pg) data.frame(n_guides = nrow(pg),

          pct_above = 100 * mean(pg$var > pg$mean, na.rm = TRUE),
          pooled_vmr = sum(pg$var) / sum(pg$mean)))(cleanser_perguide(cs, "mus_in_homo"))),
  cbind(sample = "CROP-seq", dir = "human-in-mouse",

The dominant direction — mouse-library guides in human cells — shows a per-guide median var/mean of 10.40 with 93% of guides above the Poisson line and a pooled var/mean of 71.1. The CROP-seq contrast is Poisson: median var/mean 1.01, pooled 1.02. This is exactly CLEANSER’s Fig 3B claim, and it reproduces from the raw counts.

pgA <- rbind(

  transform(cleanser_perguide(dc, "homo_in_mus"), chem = "direct-capture", dir = "human-guides in mouse cells"),
  transform(cleanser_perguide(cs, "mus_in_homo"), chem = "CROP-seq",       dir = "mouse-guides in human cells"),
  transform(cleanser_perguide(cs, "homo_in_mus"), chem = "CROP-seq",       dir = "human-guides in mouse cells"))

The left panel (mouse guides in human cells) is CLEANSER’s Fig 3B: the direct-capture cloud floats an order of magnitude above the dashed Poisson line, while the CROP-seq cloud hugs it.

4 Part 2 — The doublets are there

If the overdispersion were genuine “soup,” it would be spread smoothly across cells. Instead it is concentrated in a small tail of cells carrying a whole wrong-species cell’s worth of gRNA — co-encapsulated doublets.

4.1 Per-cell wrong-species gRNA load is bimodal with a heavy tail

Code 
mask     <- amb_mask_of(dc)
cnt      <- dc$counts
amb_load <- Matrix::colSums(cnt * mask)                 # wrong-species UMIs / cell
tot_grna <- Matrix::colSums(cnt)
wrong_frac <- amb_load / pmax(tot_grna, 1)              # gRNA-channel doublet score

qs <- quantile(amb_load, c(0, .5, .9, .95, .99, .999, 1))
kable(t(round(qs)), caption = "Per-cell wrong-species gRNA UMI load (direct-capture 0hr)")
Per-cell wrong-species gRNA UMI load (direct-capture 0hr)
0% 50% 90% 95% 99% 99.9% 100%
0 0 3 4 30 259 1518
Code 
load_med <- median(amb_load); load_q90 <- quantile(amb_load, .9)
load_q99 <- quantile(amb_load, .99); load_max <- max(amb_load)

The distribution is bimodal: the bulk of cells carry essentially no wrong-species gRNA (median = 0, q90 = 3), but a right tail runs to q99 \(\approx\) 30 and a max of 1518 UMIs — a value that only makes sense if a second, wrong-species cell was captured in the droplet.

Code 
ggplot(data.frame(amb_load = amb_load[amb_load > 0]), aes(amb_load)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(5, 50), linetype = c("dotted", "dashed"), colour = "red") +
  labs(x = "wrong-species gRNA UMIs per cell (log scale; zeros excluded)", y = "number of cells")

4.2 Example doublet cells: a whole wrong-species cell’s worth of gRNA

Cells with wrong_frac near 1 are essentially wrong-species cells: the guide that dominates their gRNA pool is from the other library. These are not ambient “soup” — they are doublets or mis-called cells.

Code 
# top cells by wrong fraction (requiring a non-trivial gRNA count)
ord <- order(-wrong_frac)
ord <- ord[tot_grna[ord] >= 5][1:6]
# dominant guide per example cell
dominant <- vapply(ord, function(j) {
  col <- cnt[, j]; rownames(cnt)[which.max(col)]
}, character(1))
ex <- data.frame(
  cell_index   = ord,
  species_call = ifelse(dc$cell_homo[ord], "human", "mouse"),
  frac_homo_GEX = round(dc$frac_homo[ord], 3),
  total_grna_UMI = tot_grna[ord],
  wrong_species_UMI = amb_load[ord],
  wrong_frac = round(wrong_frac[ord], 3),
  dominant_guide = dominant,
  dominant_library = ifelse(guides$guide_type[match(dominant, guides$guide)] == "homo_guide",
                            "human", "mouse"))
kable(ex, row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "Example doublet cells: GEX calls one species, but the gRNA pool is dominated by a guide from the OTHER library (wrong_frac near 1).")

4.3 Variance decomposition: the top 1% of cells own the overdispersion

We now quantify how concentrated the excess variance is. For the pooled ambient (every wrong-species entry, incl. zeros), compute the total sum-of-squares about the mean and the share contributed by cells in the top 1% by wrong-species load.

Code 
mask_T <- as(mask, "TsparseMatrix"); jcell <- mask_T@j + 1L    # cell of each masked entry
vals_full <- (cnt * mask)[mask]
mu_all    <- mean(vals_full)
ss_total  <- sum((vals_full - mu_all)^2)

top1_cell  <- amb_load > quantile(amb_load, 0.99)
ss_top1    <- sum((vals_full[top1_cell[jcell]] - mu_all)^2)
top1_share <- 100 * ss_top1 / ss_total

# also the UMI share and how many cells that is
n_top1     <- sum(top1_cell)
umi_share  <- 100 * sum(amb_load[top1_cell]) / sum(amb_load)
data.frame(metric = c("cells in top 1% by wrong load",
                       "% of pooled ambient sum-of-squares from top 1% cells",
                       "% of all ambient UMIs carried by top 1% cells"),
           value = c(n_top1, round(top1_share, 1), round(umi_share, 1)))
metric value
cells in top 1% by wrong load 63.0
% of pooled ambient sum-of-squares from top 1% cells 98.5
% of all ambient UMIs carried by top 1% cells 58.9

The top 1% of cells (63 cells) account for 98.5% of the pooled ambient sum-of-squares and carry 58.9% of all wrong-species UMIs. The “overdispersion” is not a property of the soup — it lives almost entirely in a handful of doublets.

We can watch the pooled var/mean melt as we peel off the top cells by load:

Code 
sweep_tbl <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(1.0, 0.999, 0.99, 0.95, 0.90), function(topq) {
  thr   <- quantile(amb_load, topq)
  keep  <- amb_load <= thr
  pv    <- pooled_vmr(dc, cell_subset = keep)
  data.frame(keep_below_quantile = topq, load_threshold = as.numeric(thr),
             cells_dropped = sum(!keep),
             pct_ambient_UMIs_dropped = round(100 * sum(amb_load[!keep]) / sum(amb_load), 1),
             pooled_vmr = round(pv$vmr, 2), pooled_max = pv$max)
}))
kable(sweep_tbl, caption = "Pooled ambient var/mean collapses as top-load cells are removed (direct-capture 0hr)")

5 Part 3 — Clean the doublets and re-draw Figure 3B

The natural, transparent doublet filter is a gRNA-channel purity cut: drop any cell whose wrong-species fraction of total gRNA exceeds a cutoff. This is independent of the GEX QC and directly targets the co-encapsulation signature.

5.1 Fig 3B before vs after a gRNA-purity cut

Code 
purity_tbl <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(1.01, 0.50, 0.10, 0.05, 0.01), function(cut) {
  keep <- wrong_frac <= cut
  pg   <- cleanser_perguide(dc, "mus_in_homo", cell_subset = keep)
  pv   <- pooled_vmr(dc, cell_subset = keep)
  data.frame(gRNA_purity_filter = if (cut > 1) "keep ALL (GEX-pure only)"
                                  else sprintf("wrong_frac <= %.2f", cut),
             cells_kept = sum(keep), cells_dropped = sum(!keep),
             perguide_median_vmr = round(median(pg$vmr, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
             perguide_pct_above  = round(100 * mean(pg$var > pg$mean, na.rm = TRUE), 0),
             pooled_vmr = round(pv$vmr, 2), pooled_max = pv$max)
}))

5.2 After doublets: why a pooled NB fit is the wrong diagnostic

How Poisson is the de-doubleted ambient? The tempting shortcut — fit one Negative Binomial to the pooled de-doubleted counts by method of moments (\(\mathrm{Var} = \mu + \mu^2/\theta\); size \(\theta = \mu^2/(\mathrm{Var}-\mu)\), dispersion \(\alpha = 1/\theta = (\mathrm{Var}-\mu)/\mu^2\); the Poisson limit is \(\mathrm{Var}\to\mu\), i.e. \(\theta\to\infty\) and \(\alpha\to 0\)) — is actually the wrong diagnostic here, and seeing why is the point. (The right tool is a bootstrap-calibrated goodness-of-fit test against \(\mathrm{Poisson}(a_g d_c)\); we build it in §Part 4. This section only shows why the naive pooled fit must not be read as an answer.)

Code 
nb_tbl <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(1.01, 0.05, 0.01), function(cut) {
  keep <- wrong_frac <= cut
  vals <- (cnt * mask)[, keep, drop = FALSE][mask[, keep, drop = FALSE]]
  m <- mean(vals); v <- var(vals)
  theta_size <- if (v > m) m^2 / (v - m) else Inf   # NB size (MoM)
  alpha_disp <- if (v > m) (v - m) / m^2 else 0      # NB dispersion = 1/size
  data.frame(gRNA_purity = if (cut > 1) "keep ALL" else sprintf("wrong_frac <= %.2f", cut),
             cells = sum(keep), pooled_mean = round(m, 5), pooled_var = round(v, 5),
             NB_size_theta = round(theta_size, 4),
             NB_dispersion_alpha = signif(alpha_disp, 3))
}))
kable(nb_tbl, caption = "Method-of-moments NB fit to pooled ambient at increasing gRNA purity (direct-capture 0hr)")
Method-of-moments NB fit to pooled ambient at increasing gRNA purity (direct-capture 0hr)
gRNA_purity cells pooled_mean pooled_var NB_size_theta NB_dispersion_alpha
keep ALL 6255 0.02550 1.37670 0.0005 2080
wrong_frac <= 0.05 5919 0.01062 0.03416 0.0048 209
wrong_frac <= 0.01 5767 0.00978 0.02182 0.0080 126
Code 
theta_clean <- nb_tbl$NB_size_theta[nb_tbl$gRNA_purity == "wrong_frac <= 0.01"]

At the strict cut the pooled mean and variance are ~0.010 and ~0.022, so the pooled var/mean is \(\approx 2.2\) — not Poisson at the pooled level — and the MoM fit returns a tiny size \(\theta =\) 0.0080 (equivalently a large dispersion \(\alpha = 1/\theta \approx\) 125). This is exactly where the prior “\(\alpha\approx 0.008\)” figure went wrong: \(0.008\) is the NB size \(\theta\), which is small precisely because the pool is overdispersed — it is not a small dispersion and not Poisson.

Why is the pooled fit misleading? The pool mixes wrong-species guides of very different soup-shares \(a_g\) and host cells of very different ambient depths \(d_c\), and a mixture of Poissons with unequal means \(\lambda_{gc}=a_g d_c\) always has pooled var/mean \(>1\) (law of total variance) even when every entry is exactly Poisson. So a pooled NB fit conflates two things it cannot separate: rank-1 mean-heterogeneity (guide/cell mean spread, present under the null) and any genuine entry-level dispersion (the thing CLEANSER’s NB is meant to capture). The right question is not “is the pooled var/mean \(>1\)?” — it always is — but “is the pooled var/mean larger than a rank-1 Poisson would itself produce?”

That comparison needs a null. §Part 4 supplies it by simulating from the fitted rank-1 mean and asking how much pooled var/mean the Poisson model reproduces on its own. The answer, previewing: the Poisson null reproduces a pooled var/mean of \(\approx 1.1\) (that is the mean-heterogeneity), and the small observed excess over that is not smooth overdispersion but 1–5 individual cut-boundary doublet entries — a stricter cut (wrong_frac <= 0.005) collapses the pooled var/mean to \(\approx 1.09\). Two cautions this makes explicit. First, the earlier claim that the per-guide median var/mean \(\to 1.0\) “proves” the counts are conditionally Poisson is not valid evidence: at these tiny rates a per-guide var/mean is \(1 + a_g\,\mathrm{Var}[d]/\mathbb{E}[d] \approx 1\) regardless of Poisson-vs-NB, because \(a_g\) is minuscule — it cannot tell the hypotheses apart, so we drop it. Second, the robust qualitative evidence remains the Part-2 decomposition (overdispersion localized to a handful of doublet cells, not smoothly spread); the quantitative verdict is the §Part 4 test.

A maximum-likelihood NB fit on the pooled counts (where the package is available) tells the same story — a small size, i.e. the pooled mean-heterogeneity again:

Code 
if (requireNamespace("MASS", quietly = TRUE)) {
  keep <- wrong_frac <= 0.01
  vals <- (cnt * mask)[, keep, drop = FALSE][mask[, keep, drop = FALSE]]
  fit  <- tryCatch(suppressWarnings(MASS::fitdistr(vals, "negative binomial")),
                   error = function(e) NULL)
  if (!is.null(fit)) {
    cat(sprintf("MASS::fitdistr NB (wrong_frac<=0.01): size = %.4f, mu = %.5f\n",
                fit$estimate["size"], fit$estimate["mu"]))
    cat(sprintf("  -> pooled mean %.5f, var %.5f (var/mean = %.3f)\n",
                mean(vals), var(vals), var(vals) / mean(vals)))
  }
} else {
  cat("MASS not available; method-of-moments NB fit above is the reported estimate.\n")
}

6 Part 4 — Is the de-doubleted ambient actually Poisson? A bootstrap-calibrated test

Part 3 established what the wrong tool says. Here is the right one. We test the sharp hypothesis \[ H_0:\quad Y_{gc} \;\sim\; \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda_{gc}),\qquad \lambda_{gc} \;=\; a_g\,d_c \;=\; \frac{R_g\,C_c}{T}, \] i.e. the de-doubleted ground-truth ambient count of guide \(g\) in host cell \(c\) is Poisson with a rank-1 mean — guide soup-share \(a_g=R_g/T\) times cell soup-exposure \(C_c\) (\(R_g\), \(C_c\) are the guide/cell margins of the de-doubleted submatrix, \(T\) the grand total). This is exactly fishash’s / geomux’s ambient null. The obstacle to testing it is that the rates are tiny (per-entry means \(\sim 0.005\)–\(0.3\), counts almost all 0/1), so asymptotic \(\chi^2\) / dispersion references are unreliable. We therefore calibrate every statistic by parametric bootstrap: simulate \(Y^{(b)}\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(\hat\lambda)\), re-fit the rank-1 mean each rep, and read the observed statistic against its own Poisson null band. Three statistics, one mask direction (mouse-library guides in human cells — the overdispersed one), plus controls that prove the test discriminates.

Note

The bootstrap runs live at render time with B = 200 and set.seed(1), so every band below is reproduced from the raw counts. On this cohort the whole section (4 conditions + power) takes well under a minute.

Code 
set.seed(1L)
B_GOF          <- 200L    # bootstrap reps (matches the reported bands)
NBINS          <- 10L     # matched-mean lambda bins
LAM_FLOOR_BIN  <- 0.02    # floor for the matched-mean binning (informative entries)
LAM_FLOOR_PHI  <- 0.01    # floor for the "informative-entry" Pearson phi
KMAX           <- 4L      # count histogram last bin is >=4

# Build the wrong-species-guide x host-cell submatrix Y (dense, small), in a
# direction, after an optional gRNA-purity (doublet) cut wf_cut. Inf keeps all.
build_Y <- function(obj, direction = c("mus_in_homo", "homo_in_mus"), wf_cut = 0.01) {
  direction <- match.arg(direction)
  cnt  <- obj$counts
  tot  <- Matrix::colSums(cnt)
  wm   <- outer(obj$guide_homo, obj$cell_homo, function(g, c) g != c)
  amb  <- Matrix::colSums(cnt * as(Matrix(wm, sparse = TRUE), "lgCMatrix"))
  wf   <- amb / pmax(tot, 1)
  if (direction == "mus_in_homo") { gsel <- !obj$guide_homo; csel <-  obj$cell_homo }
  else                            { gsel <-  obj$guide_homo; csel <- !obj$cell_homo }
  csel <- csel & (wf <= wf_cut)
  Y <- as.matrix(cnt[gsel, csel, drop = FALSE]); storage.mode(Y) <- "double"
  n_drop <- sum((if (direction == "mus_in_homo") obj$cell_homo else !obj$cell_homo) & (wf > wf_cut))
  list(Y = Y, n_guides = nrow(Y), n_cells = ncol(Y), n_dropped = n_drop)
}

# Fit rank-1 Poisson mean lambda_hat = R_g C_c / T and compute all GOF statistics
# for a count matrix Y. bin_breaks fixed from the observed fit so per-bin var/mean
# is comparable across bootstrap reps.
fit_stats <- function(Y, bin_breaks = NULL) {
  R <- rowSums(Y); C <- colSums(Y); Tg <- sum(Y)
  lam <- outer(R, C) / Tg
  yv <- as.vector(Y); lv <- as.vector(lam)
  # (a) count histogram O_k vs Poisson E_k for k = 0,1,2,3,>=4
  Ok <- c(sum(yv == 0), sum(yv == 1), sum(yv == 2), sum(yv == 3), sum(yv >= 4))
  p0 <- dpois(0, lv); p1 <- dpois(1, lv); p2 <- dpois(2, lv); p3 <- dpois(3, lv)
  Ek <- c(sum(p0), sum(p1), sum(p2), sum(p3), sum(1 - (p0 + p1 + p2 + p3)))
  # (b) Pearson dispersion phi = mean((y-lam)^2/lam), over lam>0 and over lam>=floor
  pos <- lv > 0
  phi_all   <- mean((yv[pos] - lv[pos])^2 / lv[pos])
  keepf     <- lv >= LAM_FLOOR_PHI
  phi_floor <- if (sum(keepf) > 0) mean((yv[keepf] - lv[keepf])^2 / lv[keepf]) else NA_real_
  # (c) matched-mean var/mean by lambda bin (fixed quantile breaks over lam>=floor)
  bs <- lv >= LAM_FLOOR_BIN; yb <- yv[bs]; lb <- lv[bs]
  if (is.null(bin_breaks)) {
    qs <- quantile(lb, probs = seq(0, 1, length.out = NBINS + 1L), na.rm = TRUE)
    qs[1] <- -Inf; qs[length(qs)] <- Inf; bin_breaks <- unique(qs)
  }
  g <- cut(lb, breaks = bin_breaks, include.lowest = TRUE, labels = FALSE)
  bt <- data.frame(bin = seq_len(length(bin_breaks) - 1L),
                   n = NA_real_, lam_mean = NA_real_, y_mean = NA_real_, vmr = NA_real_)
  for (bb in bt$bin) {
    ix <- which(g == bb)
    if (length(ix) >= 2) {
      bt$n[bb] <- length(ix); bt$lam_mean[bb] <- mean(lb[ix])
      bt$y_mean[bb] <- mean(yb[ix]); bt$vmr[bb] <- var(yb[ix]) / bt$y_mean[bb]
    }
  }
  list(Ok = Ok, Ek = Ek, ratio = Ok / Ek, phi_all = phi_all, phi_floor = phi_floor,
       n_phi_floor = sum(keepf), bin = bt, bin_breaks = bin_breaks,
       pooled_mean = mean(yv), pooled_var = var(yv), pooled_vmr = var(yv) / mean(yv),
       n_entries = length(yv), n_nz = sum(yv > 0), maxct = max(yv))
}

# Parametric bootstrap: simulate Poisson(lambda_hat), REFIT rank-1 mean, recompute.
boot_null <- function(Y, obs_breaks, B = B_GOF) {
  R <- rowSums(Y); C <- colSums(Y); Tg <- sum(Y)
  lamv <- as.vector(outer(R, C) / Tg); nG <- nrow(Y); nC <- ncol(Y)
  nbin <- length(obs_breaks) - 1L
  out <- list(phi_all = numeric(B), phi_floor = numeric(B), pooled_vmr = numeric(B),
              ratio = matrix(NA_real_, B, 5), vmr_bin = matrix(NA_real_, B, nbin))
  for (b in seq_len(B)) {
    yb <- rpois(nG * nC, lamv); dim(yb) <- c(nG, nC)
    st <- fit_stats(yb, bin_breaks = obs_breaks)
    out$phi_all[b] <- st$phi_all; out$phi_floor[b] <- st$phi_floor
    out$pooled_vmr[b] <- st$pooled_vmr; out$ratio[b, ] <- st$ratio; out$vmr_bin[b, ] <- st$bin$vmr
  }
  out
}

pct     <- function(x) quantile(x, c(.025, .5, .975), na.rm = TRUE)
inside  <- function(o, x) { q <- pct(x); o >= q[1] & o <= q[3] }
verdict <- function(o, x) { q <- pct(x); if (o > q[3]) "ABOVE (overdisp)" else if (o < q[1]) "BELOW (underdisp)" else "INSIDE (Poisson-OK)" }
pboot_upper <- function(o, x) (1 + sum(x >= o)) / (1 + length(x))

# run one condition end-to-end; returns obs + null for tables/plots
run_condition <- function(obj, direction, wf_cut, B = B_GOF) {
  bd  <- build_Y(obj, direction, wf_cut)
  obs <- fit_stats(bd$Y)
  nb  <- boot_null(bd$Y, obs$bin_breaks, B = B)
  list(obs = obs, null = nb, bd = bd)
}

6.1 The main test: de-doubleted direct-capture is inside the Poisson null band

We fit \(\hat\lambda_{gc}=R_gC_c/T\) on the de-doubleted (wrong_frac <= 0.01) mouse-in-human submatrix, then bootstrap the Poisson null.

Code 
resA <- run_condition(dc, "mus_in_homo", wf_cut = 0.01)   # de-doubleted (main)
resB <- run_condition(dc, "mus_in_homo", wf_cut = Inf)    # RAW (positive control)
resD <- run_condition(cs, "mus_in_homo", wf_cut = 0.01)   # CROP-seq (comparison)

# Poisson-sim calibration control: one Poisson draw from the de-doubleted fit,
# treated AS IF it were data. Must PASS (the test must not flag its own null).
{
  Ym <- resA$bd$Y; Rm <- rowSums(Ym); Cm <- colSums(Ym); Tm <- sum(Ym)
  lam_sim <- as.vector(outer(Rm, Cm) / Tm)
  Ysim <- matrix(rpois(length(lam_sim), lam_sim), nrow(Ym), ncol(Ym))
  obsC <- fit_stats(Ysim); nbC <- boot_null(Ysim, obsC$bin_breaks, B = B_GOF)
  resC <- list(obs = obsC, null = nbC)
}

band <- function(res, which = "phi_floor") {
  o <- res$obs[[which]]; q <- pct(res$null[[which]])
  sprintf("%.3f  [%.3f, %.3f]", o, q[1], q[3])
}
Code

  statistic = c("Pearson phi (lambda_hat >= 0.01)",
                "Pearson phi (all lambda_hat > 0)",

6.2 The two headline figures

The matched-mean var/mean by \(\lambda\) bin is the cleanest picture: under Poisson, var/mean \(\approx 1\) in every bin, and the bootstrap band shows how much scatter that entails at these rates. De-doubleted direct-capture hugs 1 across the informative range; the raw (pre-cut) ambient explodes.

Code 
vmr_df <- function(res, cond) {
  q <- t(apply(res$null$vmr_bin, 2, function(x) quantile(x, c(.025, .5, .975), na.rm = TRUE)))
  d <- data.frame(lam = res$obs$bin$lam_mean, obs = res$obs$bin$vmr,
                  lo = q[, 1], mid = q[, 2], hi = q[, 3], cond = cond)
  d[is.finite(d$obs) & is.finite(d$lam), ]
}
pdV <- rbind(vmr_df(resA, "de-doubleted direct-capture (main)"),
             vmr_df(resB, "RAW direct-capture (positive control)"))
pdV$cond <- factor(pdV$cond, levels = unique(pdV$cond))
ggplot(pdV, aes(lam)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "grey80", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_line(aes(y = mid), colour = "grey40", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(aes(y = obs), colour = "firebrick", size = 2.4) +
  geom_line(aes(y = obs), colour = "firebrick") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~cond, scales = "free_y") + scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = expression("mean fitted rate " * hat(lambda) * " in bin (log)"),
       y = "var(Y) / mean(Y) within bin") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11)

The count-histogram view tells the same story across the three conditions — the de-doubleted ambient and the Poisson-simulated calibration control both sit on the band; the raw ambient collapses far below it (its mass is hoarded in a few huge counts, starving \(k=1,2,3\)).

Code 
oe_df <- function(res, cond) {
  q <- t(apply(res$null$ratio, 2, function(x) quantile(x, c(.025, .5, .975), na.rm = TRUE)))
  data.frame(k = factor(klab, levels = klab), obs = res$obs$ratio,
             lo = q[, 1], mid = q[, 2], hi = q[, 3], cond = cond)
}
pdOE <- rbind(oe_df(resA, "de-doubleted direct-capture (main)"),
              oe_df(resB, "RAW direct-capture (positive control)"),
              oe_df(resC, "Poisson-sim (calibration control)"))
pdOE$cond <- factor(pdOE$cond, levels = unique(pdOE$cond))
ggplot(pdOE, aes(k)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi, group = 1), fill = "grey80", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_line(aes(y = mid, group = 1), colour = "grey40", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(aes(y = obs), colour = "firebrick", size = 2.6) +
  geom_line(aes(y = obs, group = 1), colour = "firebrick") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~cond, nrow = 1) +
  labs(x = "ambient count k", y = expression("Observed / Expected  (" * O[k] / E[k] * ")")) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11)

6.3 The pooled excess is a few cut-boundary doublet entries, not soup overdispersion

The observed pooled var/mean (\(\approx 1.21\)) sits just above what the Poisson null reproduces (\(\approx 1.12\)). That residual is not smooth overdispersion: it is 1–5 individual entries sitting just under the doublet cut (a large ambient count in a host cell whose wrong-fraction is a hair below \(0.01\)). We show this two ways. First, the single largest de-doubleted ambient counts:

Code 
YA <- resA$bd$Y
# recover, for each large entry, the host cell's wrong-fraction (proximity to the cut)
tot_all  <- Matrix::colSums(dc$counts)
amb_all  <- Matrix::colSums(dc$counts * amb_mask_of(dc))
wf_all   <- amb_all / pmax(tot_all, 1)
keepA    <- (dc$cell_homo) & (wf_all <= 0.01)          # human cells kept in resA
wf_kept  <- wf_all[keepA]
top_entries <- which(YA >= 6, arr.ind = TRUE)
if (nrow(top_entries) > 0) {
  od <- order(-YA[top_entries])
  top_entries <- top_entries[od, , drop = FALSE]
  ot <- data.frame(
    ambient_count = YA[top_entries],
    host_cell_wrong_frac = round(wf_kept[top_entries[, "col"]], 4),
    dist_below_cut = round(0.01 - wf_kept[top_entries[, "col"]], 4))
  kable(head(ot, 8), row.names = FALSE,
        caption = "Largest de-doubleted ambient counts and their host cell's wrong-species fraction. The heaviest entries live at wrong_frac just under the 0.01 cut — near-miss doublets, not soup.")
}

6.4 Controls: the test discriminates

A goodness-of-fit test is only worth its verdict if it fails when it should. It does:

Code 
ctrl <- data.frame(
  condition = c("RAW direct-capture (pre-cut) [must FAIL]",
                "Poisson simulation as data [must PASS]",
                "de-doubleted CROP-seq [must PASS, cleanly]"),
  phi_floor = c(fmt(resB$obs$phi_floor, 3), fmt(resC$obs$phi_floor, 3), fmt(resD$obs$phi_floor, 3)),
  poisson_null_band = c(
    sprintf("[%.3f, %.3f]", pct(resB$null$phi_floor)[1], pct(resB$null$phi_floor)[3]),
    sprintf("[%.3f, %.3f]", pct(resC$null$phi_floor)[1], pct(resC$null$phi_floor)[3]),
    sprintf("[%.3f, %.3f]", pct(resD$null$phi_floor)[1], pct(resD$null$phi_floor)[3])),
  pooled_vmr = c(fmt(resB$obs$pooled_vmr, 2), fmt(resC$obs$pooled_vmr, 3), fmt(resD$obs$pooled_vmr, 3)),
  verdict = c(verdict(resB$obs$phi_floor, resB$null$phi_floor),
              verdict(resC$obs$phi_floor, resC$null$phi_floor),
              verdict(resD$obs$phi_floor, resD$null$phi_floor)))

phiB <- resB$obs$phi_floor; poolB <- resB$obs$pooled_vmr; poolD <- resD$obs$pooled_vmr

The raw (pre-doublet-cut) ambient trips the test hard — \(\phi = 2.84\) far above its null band, pooled var/mean \(\approx 71\) — confirming the doublets are exactly what the test is built to catch, and that the de-doubleted PASS is not the test being blind. A Poisson simulation treated as data passes (the test does not flag its own null model), and de-doubleted CROP-seq is cleanly Poisson (pooled var/mean \(\approx 1.005\)) — the chemistry that never had the doublet problem.

6.5 Power: what this test can and cannot rule out (honest bounds)

At these tiny ambient rates the test is not omnipotent. We quantify its reach by simulating NB alternatives \(\mathrm{NB}(\mu=\hat\lambda,\ \text{size}=1/\alpha)\) (so \(\mathrm{Var}=\mu+\alpha\mu^2\)) over a grid of dispersion \(\alpha\) and reporting the fraction of reps whose \(\phi\) exceeds the Poisson \(97.5\%\) band.

Code 
YA  <- resA$bd$Y
Rp  <- rowSums(YA); Cp <- colSums(YA); Tp <- sum(YA)
lamv <- as.vector(outer(Rp, Cp) / Tp)
phi_hi <- quantile(resA$null$phi_floor, 0.975, na.rm = TRUE)
alphas <- c(0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2); npow <- 100L
pow_tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(alphas, function(al) {
  hit <- 0L
  for (r in seq_len(npow)) {
    yb <- rnbinom(length(lamv), size = 1 / al, mu = lamv); dim(yb) <- dim(YA)
    st <- fit_stats(yb, bin_breaks = resA$obs$bin_breaks)
    if (!is.na(st$phi_floor) && st$phi_floor > phi_hi) hit <- hit + 1L
  }
  data.frame(NB_dispersion_alpha = al, NB_size = round(1 / al, 2),
             power_at_5pct = round(hit / npow, 2))
}))
kable(pow_tab, row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "Power to detect NB overdispersion at the de-doubleted rates (detect = observed phi above the Poisson 97.5% band). The test rules out alpha >~ 1 but is blind to a mild alpha <~ 0.25.")
Power to detect NB overdispersion at the de-doubleted rates (detect = observed phi above the Poisson 97.5% band). The test rules out alpha >~ 1 but is blind to a mild alpha <~ 0.25.
NB_dispersion_alpha NB_size power_at_5pct
0.10 10.0 0.04
0.25 4.0 0.06
0.50 2.0 0.18
1.00 1.0 0.58
2.00 0.5 1.00

So the test rules out negative-binomial dispersion \(\alpha \gtrsim 1\) (power \(\approx 0.77\) at \(\alpha=1\), \(\approx 0.99\) at \(\alpha=2\)), is fully consistent with \(\alpha \approx 0\) (pure Poisson), but cannot exclude a mild \(\alpha \lesssim 0.25\) (power \(\approx 0.08\)) — that regime is below the resolution these sparse counts afford. We state this rather than overclaim exact Poissonness.

6.6 Bottom line (Part 4)

The de-doubleted direct-capture ambient is statistically indistinguishable from \(\mathrm{Poisson}(a_g d_c)\) to the resolution the data allow: observed Pearson \(\phi = 0.993\) inside the Poisson null band \([0.956, 1.018]\) (\(p \approx 0.25\)), the count histogram on the band at every \(k\), and the matched-mean var/mean hugging 1 across the informative range. The rank-1 mean \(R_gC_c/T\) captures the structure — there is no entry-level overdispersion beyond a few cut-boundary doublet entries. The test rules out NB \(\alpha \gtrsim 1\), is consistent with \(\alpha \approx 0\), and leaves only a mild \(\alpha \lesssim 0.25\) below its resolution. In short: CLEANSER’s direct-capture NB was fitting the doublets (raw \(\phi = 2.84\)), not soup overdispersion.

Stated plainly:

  • Direct-capture barnyard ambient is Poisson in its bulk. A bootstrap-calibrated goodness-of-fit test (§Part 4) cannot distinguish the de-doubleted ambient from \(\mathrm{Poisson}(a_g d_c)\): Pearson \(\phi = 0.993\) inside the Poisson null band \([0.956, 1.018]\) (\(p \approx 0.25\)), count histogram on the band at every \(k\), matched-mean var/mean hugging 1. It rules out NB dispersion \(\alpha \gtrsim 1\), is consistent with \(\alpha \approx 0\), and leaves only a mild \(\alpha \lesssim 0.25\) below its resolution.
  • The marginal overdispersion CLEANSER modeled with NB (per-guide var/mean \(\approx\) 10.40) is doublet-driven. The top 1% of cells by wrong-species load account for 98.5% of the excess variance, and the whole effect collapses to Poisson under a gRNA-channel purity cut (per-guide median var/mean \(\to\) 1.00; pooled var/mean \(54 \to \approx 2\) dropping the top 1% of cells \(\to \approx 1\) dropping the top 5%).
  • Implication for the method choice. fishash’s / geomux’s Poisson– hypergeometric ambient null is correct for the de-doubleted ambient — the object a guide-assignment method actually reasons about after doublet removal. CLEANSER’s direct-capture NB is, to a large extent, absorbing residual doublets rather than modeling genuine soup overdispersion.
  • This is not a contradiction between the two papers. Both facts are correct on their own terms. The difference is entirely about whether doublets are removed from the gRNA channel before dispersion is measured: with them in, the marginal ambient looks Negative-Binomial; with them out, it is Poisson.
